step1_analysis.description: A pseudo-differential delay cell for a continuous-time FIR filter. Each half uses a transconductor and an active feedback network (likely forming an active inductor or 2nd-order low-pass filter) to synthesize a tunable delay.

paper_reference.title: A CMOS 0.25-m Continuous-Time FIR Filter With 125 ps per Tap Delay as a Fractionally Spaced Receiver Equalizer for 1-Gb/s Data Transmission

sky130_expected.calculation: Expected to be similar to the paper's reported 125 ps, tunable between 100 ps and 300 ps.
sky130_expected.reasoning: The delay is determined by the active inductor and load capacitance, which can be tuned. Sky130 is faster than 0.25um, so similar or lower delays are easily achievable.

sky130_expected.calculation: Paper reports 2.1 GHz at 100 ps delay and 800 MHz at 300 ps delay.
sky130_expected.reasoning: Bandwidth is inversely proportional to the delay. Sky130 can easily achieve >2GHz bandwidth.

sky130_expected.calculation: 45 mW / 6 taps = 7.5 mW per tap. At 1.8V, this is ~4.1 mA.
sky130_expected.reasoning: Power scales with technology and supply voltage. 1.8V in Sky130 will likely consume similar power to achieve the same bandwidth.

sky130_expected.calculation: Delay cells in FIR filters typically have unity gain (0 dB) to prevent signal saturation across multiple taps.
sky130_expected.reasoning: Unity gain is standard for delay lines.

step3_testbench.description: Testbench to measure delay, bandwidth, gain, and power consumption of the continuous-time FIR filter delay cell.
